title: Senior's toolkit: grouping and joining
summary: Named aggregations, transform, pivot tables, merges that check themselves, concat and melt.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: grouping and joining
steps.body: Summaries and joins are where report numbers go wrong without any error: a duplicated key doubles revenue, a missing key drops customers. These are the forms experienced analysts use, with the checks built in.

toolkit.what: Named aggregations: you choose each output column's name, and get a flat table ready to report or join.
flags: keep the group keys as columns, not the index
keep a group for missing keys instead of dropping those rows

toolkit.what: A group result repeated on every row of the group, so you can compare each row with its group (share of region, difference from the mean).
flags: the group total on each row
the group mean on each row

toolkit.what: A spreadsheet-style summary: rows by one key, columns by another.
flags: how to combine values (the default is mean)
show 0 instead of NaN for empty cells
add an All row and column with totals
toolkit.example: df.pivot_table(index="region", columns="quarter", values="amount", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0, margins=True)

toolkit.what: Count combinations of two categories, optionally as shares.
Join two tables and make pandas check your assumption about the keys. Without `validate`, duplicate keys silently multiply rows.
flags: keep every row of the left table
raise MergeError if the right table has duplicate keys
names for columns that exist on both sides

toolkit.what: Stack tables with the same columns, for example one file per month. (`df.append` was removed in pandas 2.)
flags: remember which table each row came from
toolkit.example: year = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(p) for p in sorted(Path("data").glob("2026-*.csv"))], ignore_index=True)

toolkit.what: Wide to long: turn one column per month into rows of (month, value), the tidy shape groupby and plotting expect.
flags: columns to keep as they are
name for the old column headers

steps.prompt: After joining orders to the price list, total revenue is 2.3 times what the ledger says. No error was raised. What happened, and how do you make it impossible next time?
options: Some products appear more than once in the price list, so their orders were duplicated; add `validate="many_to_one"` so the merge raises, then deduplicate the price list
`merge` adds the price twice by design; divide by 2
The ledger is wrong; trust the merge
steps.explain: A key that matches 3 rows on the right turns 1 order into 3. `validate=` states your assumption and fails loudly when the data breaks it. Also compare `len()` before and after any merge.

steps.prompt: You merge orders with customers using `how="left", indicator=True`, and `df["_merge"].value_counts()` shows `left_only 120`. What does that mean?
options: 120 orders found no matching customer: check those keys (missing customers, different types such as `"42"` vs `42`, or stray spaces)
steps.explain: `left_only` rows exist only in the left table. Their customer columns are NaN, so any per-customer report quietly loses them. Look at a few with `df[df["_merge"] == "left_only"]`.

steps.prompt: Join orders to customers, fail if a customer id is duplicated, and mark which orders had no match.
steps.explain: `validate` checks the key relationship; `indicator` adds the `_merge` column.
Each named aggregation becomes one column, and `as_index=False` keeps `region` as an ordinary column.

steps.prompt: Match each argument to its effect.
pairs: missing keys get their own group
adds an All row and column

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Write `validate=` on every merge and compare row counts before and after; check `_merge` whenever a left join could miss keys. Use named aggregations so the output columns say what they are, and reconcile one total against a trusted source before you share a report.
